2 Preliminaries We write $\|\cdot\|$ for the Euclidean norm and $I_{d}$ for the $d\times d$ identity matrix.
For symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$ , the notation $A\preceq B$ means that $B-A$ is positive semidefinite. Let $O(n):=\{O\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}:O^{\top}O=I_{n}\}$ denote the real orthogonal group, equipped with Haar probability
measure.
It has two components, $\{\det O=+1\}$ , $\{\det O=-1\}$ , and each have Haar probability $1/2$ .
For $b\in\{-1,+1\}$ , we write $\mu_{n,b}$ for Haar probability
measure conditioned on $\det O=b$ . Targets and oracle. We restrict the target class to centered Gaussians.
This restriction removes the hardness of locating the target and isolates the difficulty of sampling with an unknown covariance.
For an integer $d\geq 1$ and a parameter $\kappa\geq 1$ , without loss of generality, we normalize the spectral bounds to $1$ and $\kappa$ by rescaling and consider
the precision class $\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}:=\left\{A\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}:A=A^{\top},\quad I_{d}\preceq A\preceq\kappa I_{d}\right\}.$ An input $A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}$ specifies the quadratic
potential $f_{A}(x):=\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax$ and the target distribution $\pi_{A}:=N(0,A^{-1})$ .
At a point $x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , the exact first-order oracle returns $\operatorname{FO}_{A}(x):=\bigl(f_{A}(x),\nabla f_{A}(x)\bigr)=\left(\frac{1}{2}x^{\top}Ax,Ax\right).$ (1) On this class, exact first-order access is equivalent to exact
matrix–vector access.
Indeed, a first-order response contains $Ax$ , while a
matrix–vector response determines both the gradient $Ax$ and the function value $\frac{1}{2}\langle x,Ax\rangle$ .
Thus the exact value-and-gradient, gradient-only, and
matrix–vector query complexities coincide. Randomized algorithms. A randomized algorithm chooses its queries and stopping decisions
as Borel functions of its internal randomness and previous oracle
responses, where the randomness is independent of the input.
Its output may be any $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ -valued Borel function of
the same information.
The algorithm has fixed query budget $T$ if it makes
at most $T$ queries for every admissible input and every
realization of its internal randomness. Accuracy measures. For probability measures $P$ and $Q$ on a common measurable space,
their total variation distance is $\operatorname{TV}(P,Q):=\sup_{B}|P(B)-Q(B)|=\frac{1}{2}\int|p-q|\,d\lambda,$ where the supremum ranges over measurable sets, and $p$ and $q$ are the densities of $P$ and $Q$ with respect to any common
dominating measure $\lambda$ .
In particular, $|\mathbb{E}_{P}h-\mathbb{E}_{Q}h|\leq\operatorname{TV}(P,Q)$ for every measurable function $h$ taking values in $[0,1]$ . Sampling accuracy and query complexity. For a fixed input $A$ , let $\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}$ denote
the law of the algorithm’s output, with all internal
randomness included.
For $0<\varepsilon<1$ , define $Q_{G}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon):=\inf\left\{T\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}:\begin{array}[]{l}\exists\,\mathrm{Alg}\text{ with fixed query budget }T\\[2.0pt]
\text{such that }\displaystyle\sup_{A\in\mathcal{A}_{d,\kappa}}\operatorname{TV}\bigl(\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}},\pi_{A}\bigr)\leq\varepsilon\end{array}\right\}.$ (2) The accuracy requirement is uniform over inputs and concerns
the output law after averaging over the algorithm’s seed.
Throughout the paper, query budgets are deterministic caps
on the number of queries in each run, rather than bounds
on the expected number of queries.

B.1 Indistinguishability: Proof of Lemma 3.2 In this section, we prove Lemma 3.2 .
Throughout this section, $2T<n$ . Lemma B.1 ( Indistinguishability (Lemma 5 restated)). For every randomized first-order algorithm $\mathrm{Alg}$ with query budget $T<n/2$ , $\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{D}_{+1}}[\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}]=\mathbb{E}_{A\sim\mathcal{D}_{-1}}[\rho_{A}^{\mathrm{Alg}}].$ (13) Oracle reduction. Consider the oracle $\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{O}}(j,v,\tau):=\begin{cases}O_{j}v,&\tau=\mathsf{f},\\
O_{j}^{\top}v,&\tau=\mathsf{i},\end{cases}\qquad j\in\{1,\ldots,k\},\quad v\in\mathbb{R}^{n}.$ We call a query $(j,v,\tau)$ to
this oracle a primitive query; it is forward if $\tau=\mathsf{f}$ ,
and inverse if $\tau=\mathsf{i}$ .
For a first-order query $x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k},z)$ , we have $\displaystyle A_{O_{j}}x_{j}$ $\displaystyle=\frac{\kappa+1}{2}x_{j}-\frac{\kappa-1}{4}\bigl(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{O}}(j,x_{j},\mathsf{f})+\mathcal{O}_{\mathbf{O}}(j,x_{j},\mathsf{i})\bigr),$ $\displaystyle\nabla f_{A_{\mathbf{O}}}(x)$ $\displaystyle=(A_{O_{1}}x_{1},\ldots,A_{O_{k}}x_{k},z),$ $\displaystyle f_{A_{\mathbf{O}}}(x)$ $\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\langle x,\nabla f_{A_{\mathbf{O}}}(x)\rangle.$ Thus $T$ first-order queries can be simulated using at most $2T$ primitive queries per block and it suffices to prove transcript
indistinguishability for adaptive primitive queries when $2T<n$ . Single-observation Haar laws. When at least two dimensions remain, a forward or inverse observation
has a sign-independent law. The following lemma also identifies the
conditional Haar law of the remaining map. Lemma B.2 ( Conditional law of $W$ given $Wu$ ). Let $m\geq 2$ , $b\in\{-1,+1\}$ , and $W\sim\mu_{m,b}$ .
Write $\sigma_{m-1}$ for uniform probability measure on $S^{m-1}$ .
Choose Borel maps $z\mapsto Q_{z}\in SO(m)$ satisfying $Q_{z}e_{1}=z$ .
For every $u\in S^{m-1}$ , $Wu\sim\sigma_{m-1},\qquad\mathcal{L}(W\mid Wu=z)=\mathcal{L}\!\left(Q_{z}\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&V\end{pmatrix}Q_{u}^{\top}\right),\quad V\sim\mu_{m-1,b},$ for $\sigma_{m-1}$ -almost every $z$ .
The same identities hold with $W$ replaced by $W^{\top}$ . Proof. The Borel completions $Q_{z}$ can be obtained by fixed-order
Gram–Schmidt, followed by a sign correction on the last column.
Let $Z\sim\sigma_{m-1}$ and $V\sim\mu_{m-1,b}$ be independent, and set $\widetilde{W}:=Q_{Z}\operatorname{diag}(1,V)Q_{u}^{\top}$ .
Then $\widetilde{W}u=Z$ and $\det\widetilde{W}=b$ . For $R\in SO(m)$ , $Q_{Rz}^{\top}RQ_{z}=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\
0&S_{R}(z)\end{pmatrix},\qquad S_{R}(z)\in SO(m-1).$ Rotational invariance of $Z$ and Haar invariance of $V$ give $(RZ,S_{R}(Z)V)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}(Z,V)$ , hence $R\widetilde{W}=Q_{RZ}\operatorname{diag}(1,S_{R}(Z)V)Q_{u}^{\top}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\widetilde{W}.$ Thus $\widetilde{W}\sim\mu_{m,b}$ by uniqueness of invariant
probability measure on the determinant component.
Since $\widetilde{W}u=Z$ , conditioning on $Z=z$ yields both identities.
Finally, $W^{\top}\sim\mu_{m,b}$ , so the same argument applies to
inverse observations.
∎ Adaptive posterior laws. We now apply Lemma B.2 to adaptive queries
across blocks, maintaining the conditional Haar law of each residual map. Lemma B.3 ( Adaptive posterior factorization). Fix $b\in\{-1,+1\}$ and let $O_{1},\ldots,O_{k}$ be independent
with law $\mu_{n,b}$ .
Consider a deterministic adaptive primitive-query algorithm making
at most $2T<n$ queries to each block.
Let $H_{t}$ be its complete history and $\ell_{j,t}$ the number of
queries to block $j$ .
There exist history-measurable frames $Q_{D,j,t},Q_{R,j,t}\in SO(n)$ and integers $r_{j,t}\leq\ell_{j,t}$ such that $O_{j}=Q_{R,j,t}\operatorname{diag}(I_{r_{j,t}},W_{j,t})Q_{D,j,t}^{\top},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{b}\bigl((W_{j,t})_{j=1}^{k}\mid H_{t}=h\bigr)=\bigotimes_{j=1}^{k}\mu_{n-r_{j,t}(h),b}.$ The frames and exposed dimensions are chosen by rules independent of $b$ . Proof. At $t=0$ , take $Q_{D,j,0}=Q_{R,j,0}=I_{n}$ , $r_{j,0}=\ell_{j,0}=0$ ,
and $W_{j,0}=O_{j}$ .
The assertion follows from the independence of the blocks. Assume the assertion holds at time $t$ .
Fix a nonterminal history $h$ and its next query $(j,v,\tau)$ .
For the selected block, suppress $j,t$ and write $Q_{D}=[U_{D},E]$ , $Q_{R}=[U_{R},F]$ , and $m=n-r$ .
The two query types give $\begin{array}[]{lll}\tau=\mathsf{f}:&v=U_{D}a+Ec,&Y=U_{R}a+FWc,\\
\tau=\mathsf{i}:&v=U_{R}a+Fc,&Y=U_{D}a+EW^{\top}c.\end{array}$ Here $a\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$ and $c\in\mathbb{R}^{m}$ are the coordinates of $v$ in the corresponding frame: $a=U_{D}^{\top}v$ , $c=E^{\top}v$ for a forward
query, and $a=U_{R}^{\top}v$ , $c=F^{\top}v$ for an inverse query.
If $c=0$ , the response $Y$ is determined by $h$ , so the query reveals
nothing about $W$ . In this case we leave the frames, the exposed
dimension, and the residual map unchanged. Suppose $c\neq 0$ . The algorithm makes at most $2T$ queries to each block,
and the next query is addressed to block $j$ , so $\ell_{j,t}\leq 2T-1$ .
Together with $r\leq\ell_{j,t}$ and $2T<n$ , this gives $m=n-r\geq n-2T+1\geq 2.$ Write $c=\|c\|u$ with $u\in S^{m-1}$ . For a forward query, $Y=U_{R}a+\|c\|\,F(Wu)$ , so given $h$ the response $Y$ and the vector $z:=Wu=F^{\top}Y/\|c\|$ determine each other. For an inverse query the
same holds with $z:=W^{\top}u=E^{\top}Y/\|c\|$ .
By Lemma B.2 , conditionally on this response, $\begin{array}[]{ll}W=Q_{z}\operatorname{diag}(1,V)Q_{u}^{\top},&\tau=\mathsf{f},\\
W^{\top}=Q_{z}\operatorname{diag}(1,V)Q_{u}^{\top},&\tau=\mathsf{i},\end{array}\qquad V\sim\mu_{m-1,b}.$ Put $B_{u}=\operatorname{diag}(I_{r},Q_{u})$ and $B_{z}=\operatorname{diag}(I_{r},Q_{z})$ , and update $(Q_{D}^{+},Q_{R}^{+},W^{+})=\begin{cases}(Q_{D}B_{u},Q_{R}B_{z},V),&\tau=\mathsf{f},\\
(Q_{D}B_{z},Q_{R}B_{u},V^{\top}),&\tau=\mathsf{i}.\end{cases}$ In both cases, $O_{j}=Q_{R}^{+}\operatorname{diag}(I_{r+1},W^{+})(Q_{D}^{+})^{\top},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{b}(W^{+}\mid H_{t}=h,Y)=\mu_{m-1,b}.$ All updated frames belong to $SO(n)$ and depend only on $(h,Y)$ . Leave the other blocks unchanged and set $r_{i}^{+}=r_{i}+\mathbf{1}_{\{i=j\}}\mathbf{1}_{\{c\neq 0\}}$ .
